nodes.name: pro-representable functor
nodes.statement:
A covariant functor $F$ from $\boldsymbol{C}$ to Sets is called pro-representable if it has the form
\end{enumerate}

$$
F(A) \cong \operatorname{Hom}_{\text {local } \Lambda \text {-alg. }}(R, A), \quad A \in C,
$$

where $R$ is a complete local $\Lambda$-algebra such that $R / \boldsymbol{m}^{n}$ is in $\boldsymbol{C}$, all $n$. ( $\boldsymbol{m}$ is the maximal ideal in $R$.)
nodes.statement_short: $F$ is pro-representable if $F \cong \operatorname{Hom}(R,\cdot)$ for a complete local $\Lambda$-algebra $R$ with all $R/m^n$ in $C$.

nodes.name: base ring Lambda, maximal ideal mu, residue field k

nodes.name: category C_Lambda of Artinian local Lambda-algebras
nodes.statement: We define $\boldsymbol{C}=\boldsymbol{C}_{\Lambda}$ to be the category of Artinian local $\Lambda$-algebras having residue field $k$. (That is, the "structure morphism" $\Lambda \rightarrow A$ of such a ring $A$ induces a trivial extension of residue fields.) Morphisms in $C$ are local homomorphisms of $\Lambda$-algebras.

nodes.name: fibre product of rings
nodes.statement: If $p: A \rightarrow B, q: C \rightarrow B$ are morphisms in $C$, let $A \times_{B} C$ denote the ring (in $C$ ) consisting of all pairs $(a, c)$ with $a \in A, c \in C$, for which $p a=q c$, with coordinatewise multiplication and addition.

nodes.name: Lemma 1.1 (surjectivity criterion via cotangent spaces)
nodes.statement: Lemma 1.1. A morphism $B \rightarrow A$ in $\hat{\boldsymbol{C}}$ is surjective if and only if the induced map from $t_{B}^{*}$ to $t_{A}^{*}$ is surjective.
conclusions: A morphism $B \rightarrow A$ in $\hat{\boldsymbol{C}}$ is surjective if and only if the induced map from $t_{B}^{*}$ to $t_{A}^{*}$ is surjective
equivalent_conditions: A morphism $B \rightarrow A$ in $\hat{\boldsymbol{C}}$ is surjective

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 1.1
nodes.statement:
Proof. First of all, any $A$ in $\hat{C}$ is generated, as $\Lambda$ module, by the image of $\Lambda$ in $A$ and the maximal ideal $\boldsymbol{m}$ of $A$. (For $A$ and $\Lambda$ have the same residue field $k$.) Thus the induced map from $\mu / \mu^{2}$ to $\mu A /\left(\boldsymbol{m}^{2} \cap \mu A\right)$ is a surjection. If $B \rightarrow A$ is a morphism in $\hat{\boldsymbol{C}}$, then denoting the maximal ideal of $B$ by $\boldsymbol{n}$, we get a commutative diagram with exact rows:\\
\includegraphics[max width=\textwidth, alt={}, center]{133f4430-1007-4a22-9674-9093b9475bf3-02_188_762_1277_452}\\
in which the left-hand arrow is a surjection. If the right-hand arrow is also a surjection, then the middle arrow is a surjection, so that the induced map on the graded rings is a surjection. From this it follows that $B \rightarrow A$ is a surjection [1, §2, No. 8, Theorem 1].

Conversely, if $B \rightarrow A$ is a surjection, then the induced map on cotangent spaces is obviously surjective.
nodes.statement_short: Compare exact sequences of cotangent data; surjectivity on graded rings gives surjectivity (Bourbaki).

nodes.statement_short: Any $A$ is generated by the image of $\Lambda$ and $m$, so $\mu/\mu^2\to\mu A/(m^2\cap\mu A)$ is onto.

nodes.name: essential surjection
nodes.statement: Definition 1.3. $p$ is essential if for any morphism $q: C \rightarrow B$ in $C$ such that $p q$ is surjective, it follows that $q$ is surjective.
differentia: for any morphism $q: C \rightarrow B$ in $C$ such that $p q$ is surjective, it follows that $q$ is surjective

nodes.name: Lemma 1.4 (essential surjections and small extensions)
nodes.statement:
Lemma 1.4. Let $p: B \rightarrow A$ be a surjection in $C$. Then

\begin{itemize}
  \item[(i)] $p$ is essential if and only if the induced map $p_{*}: t_{B}^{*} \rightarrow t_{A}^{*}$ is an isomorphism.
  \item[(ii)] If $p$ is a small extension, then $p$ is not essential if and only if $p$ has a section $s: A \rightarrow B$, with $p s=1_{A}$.
assumptions: $p: B \rightarrow A$ be a surjection in $C$
conclusions: $p$ is essential if and only if the induced map $p_{*}: t_{B}^{*} \rightarrow t_{A}^{*}$ is an isomorphism
$p$ is not essential if and only if $p$ has a section $s: A \rightarrow B$, with $p s=1_{A}$
$p$ is essential if and only if the induced map $p_{*}: t_{B}^{*} \rightarrow t_{A}^{*}$ is an isomorphism
$p$ is not essential if and only if $p$ has a section $s: A \rightarrow B$, with $p s=1_{A}$

nodes.statement_short: A surjection is essential iff it is an iso on cotangent spaces; a small extension is non-essential iff it has a section.

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 1.4
nodes.statement:
Proof. (i) If $p_{*}$ is an isomorphism, then by Lemma 1.1, $p$ is essential. Conversely let $\tilde{t}_{1}, \ldots, \tilde{t}_{r}$ be a basis of $t_{A}^{*}$, and lift the $\tilde{t}_{i}$ back to elements $t_{i}$ in $B$. Set

$$
C=\Lambda\left[t_{1}, \ldots, t_{r}\right] \subseteq B .
$$

Then $p$ induces a surjection from $C$ to $A$, so if $p$ is essential, $C=B$. But then $\operatorname{dim}_{k} t_{B}^{*} \leqq r=\operatorname{dim}_{k} t_{A}^{*}$, so $t_{B}^{*} \cong t_{A}^{*}$.\\
(ii) If $p$ has a section $s$, then $s$ is not surjective, so $p$ is not essential. If $p$ is not essential, then the subring $C$ constructed above is a proper subring of $B$, and hence is isomorphic to $A$, since length $(B)=$ length $(A)+1$. The isomorphism $C \cong A$ yields the section.
nodes.statement_short: Lift a basis of $t_A^*$ to build the subring $C=\Lambda[t_1,\dots,t_r]\subseteq B$ mapping onto $A$; compare dimensions and lengths.

nodes.name: functors with F(k) a single point
nodes.statement: We shall consider only ccvariant functors $F$, from $\boldsymbol{C}$ to Sets, such that $F(k)$ contains just one element.

nodes.name: couple for a functor
nodes.statement: By a couple for $F$ we mean a pair $(A, \xi)$ where $A \in C$ and $\xi \in F(A)$.

nodes.name: morphism of couples
nodes.statement: A morphism of couples $u:(A, \xi) \rightarrow\left(A^{\prime}, \xi^{\prime}\right)$ is a morphism $u: A \rightarrow A^{\prime}$ in $\boldsymbol{C}$ such that $F(u)(\xi)=\xi^{\prime}$.

nodes.statement: If we extend $F$ to $\hat{\boldsymbol{C}}$ by the formula $\hat{F}(A)=$ proj $\operatorname{Lim} F\left(A / \boldsymbol{m}^{n}\right)$ we may speak analogously of pro-couples and morphisms of pro-couples.

nodes.name: functor h_R
nodes.statement: For any ring $R$ in $\hat{\boldsymbol{C}}$, we set $h_{R}(A)=\operatorname{Hom}(R, A)$ to define a functor $h_{R}$ on $C$.

nodes.name: Yoneda-type isomorphism F-hat(R) = Hom(h_R, F)
nodes.statement:
Now if $F$ is any functor on $C$, and $R$ is in $\hat{\boldsymbol{C}}$, we have a canonical isomorphism

$$
\hat{F}(R) \xrightarrow{\sim} \operatorname{Hom}\left(h_{R}, F\right) .
$$
conclusions: we have a canonical isomorphism
nodes.statement_short: Pro-objects of $F$ over $R$ correspond to natural transformations $h_R\to F$.

nodes.name: Proof of the isomorphism F-hat(R) = Hom(h_R, F)

Then each $u: R \rightarrow A$ factors through $u_{n}: R / \boldsymbol{m}^{n} \rightarrow \mathcal{A}$ for some $n$, and we assign to $u \in h_{R}(A)$ the element $F\left(u_{n}\right)\left(\xi_{n}\right)$ of $F(A)$. This sets up the isomorphism.
nodes.statement_short: Each $u:R\to A$ factors through some $R/m^n$; send $u$ to $F(u_n)(\xi_n)$.

nodes.name: pro-couple pro-represents F
nodes.statement: We therefore say that a pro-couple $(R, \xi)$ for $F$ pro-represents $F$ if the morphism $h_{R} \rightarrow F$ induced by $\xi$ is an isomorphism.

nodes.name: Relation to global functors (2.1)
nodes.statement: (2.1) Relation to global functors. Let $G$ be a contravariant functor on the category of preschemes over Spec $\Lambda$, and pick a fixed $e \in G(\operatorname{Spec} k)$. For $A$ in $C$, let $F(A) \subseteq G(\operatorname{Spec} A)$ be the set of those $\xi \in G(\operatorname{Spec} A)$ such that $G(i)(\xi)=e$ where $i$ is the inclusion of $\operatorname{Spec} k$ in $\operatorname{Spec} A$. If $G$ is represented by a prescheme $X$, then $e$ determines a $k$-rational point $x \in X$, and it is then clear that $F(A)$ is isomorphic to $\operatorname{Hom}_{\Lambda}\left(\mathfrak{O}_{X, x}, A\right)$. Thus the completion of $\mathfrak{O}_{X, x}$ pro-represents $F$.
nodes.statement_short: A functor $G$ on preschemes with base point gives a local functor $F$; if $G$ is representable by $X$, $\hat{\mathcal O}_{X,x}$ pro-represents $F$.

nodes.name: smooth morphism of functors
nodes.statement_short: $F\to G$ is smooth if $F(B)\to F(A)\times_{G(A)}G(B)$ is onto for every surjection $B\to A$.

nodes.name: Remark 2.4 (smooth implies surjective on pro-objects)
nodes.statement: (2.4) If $F \rightarrow G$ is smooth, then $\hat{F} \rightarrow \hat{G}$ is surjective, in the sense that $\hat{F}(A) \rightarrow \hat{G}(A)$ is surjective for all $A$ in $\hat{\boldsymbol{C}}$ (consider the successive quotients $A / \boldsymbol{m}^{n}, n=1,2, \ldots$ ).
conclusions: $\hat{F} \rightarrow \hat{G}$ is surjective, in the sense that $\hat{F}(A) \rightarrow \hat{G}(A)$ is surjective for all $A$ in $\hat{\boldsymbol{C}}$

nodes.name: Proposition 2.5 (sorites on smooth morphisms)
nodes.statement:
Proposition 2.5. (i) Let $R \rightarrow S$ be a morphism in $\hat{\boldsymbol{C}}$. Then $h_{S} \rightarrow h_{R}$ is smooth if and only if $S$ is a power series ring over $R$.\\
(ii) If $F \rightarrow G$ and $G \rightarrow H$ are smooth morphisms of functors, then the composition $F \rightarrow H$ is smooth.\\
(iii) If $u: F \rightarrow G$ and $v: G \rightarrow H$ are morphisms of functors such that $u$ is surjective and $v u$ is smooth, then $v$ is smooth.\\
(iv) If $F \rightarrow G$ and $H \rightarrow G$ are morphisms of functors such that $F \rightarrow G$ is smooth, then $F \times_{G} H \rightarrow H$ is smooth.
nodes.statement_short: Smoothness: $h_S\to h_R$ smooth iff $S$ power series over $R$; stable under composition, quotients by surjections and base change.

nodes.name: Proposition 2.5 (i): h_S -> h_R smooth iff S power series ring over R
nodes.statement: (i) Let $R \rightarrow S$ be a morphism in $\hat{\boldsymbol{C}}$. Then $h_{S} \rightarrow h_{R}$ is smooth if and only if $S$ is a power series ring over $R$.

nodes.name: Proposition 2.5 (ii): composition of smooth morphisms
nodes.statement: (ii) If $F \rightarrow G$ and $G \rightarrow H$ are smooth morphisms of functors, then the composition $F \rightarrow H$ is smooth.
assumptions: $F \rightarrow G$ and $G \rightarrow H$ are smooth morphisms of functors
conclusions: the composition $F \rightarrow H$ is smooth

nodes.name: Proposition 2.5 (iii): smoothness descends along surjections
nodes.statement: (iii) If $u: F \rightarrow G$ and $v: G \rightarrow H$ are morphisms of functors such that $u$ is surjective and $v u$ is smooth, then $v$ is smooth.
assumptions: $u: F \rightarrow G$ and $v: G \rightarrow H$ are morphisms of functors such that $u$ is surjective and $v u$ is smooth
conclusions: $v$ is smooth

nodes.name: Proposition 2.5 (iv): base change of smooth morphisms
nodes.statement: (iv) If $F \rightarrow G$ and $H \rightarrow G$ are morphisms of functors such that $F \rightarrow G$ is smooth, then $F \times_{G} H \rightarrow H$ is smooth.

conclusions: $F \times_{G} H \rightarrow H$ is smooth

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition 2.5
nodes.statement:
Proof. (i) This is more or less well known (see [3, Theorem 3.1]), but we give a proof for the sake of completeness. Suppose $h_{S} \rightarrow h_{R}$ is smooth. Let $r$ (resp. $s$ ) be the maximal ideal in $R$ (resp. $S$ ), and pick $x_{1}, \ldots, x_{n}$ in $S$ which induce a basis of $t_{S / R}^{*}=s /\left(s^{2}+r S\right)$. If we set $T=R\left[\left[X_{1}, \ldots, X_{n}\right]\right]$ and denote the maximal ideal of $T$ by $t$, we get a morphism $u_{1}: S \rightarrow T /\left(t^{2}+r T\right)$ of local $R$ algebras, obtained by mapping $x_{i}$ on the residue class of $X_{i}$. By smoothness $u_{1}$ lifts to $u_{2}: S \rightarrow T / t^{2}$, thence to $u_{3}: S \rightarrow T / t^{3}, \ldots$ etc. Thus we get a $u: S \rightarrow T$ which induces an isomorphism of $t_{S / R}^{*}$ with $t_{T / R}^{*}$ (by choice of $u_{1}$ ) so that $u$ is a surjection (1.1). Furthermore, if we choose $y_{i} \in S$ such that $u y_{i}=X_{i}$, we can set $v X_{i}=y_{i}$ and produce a local morphism $v: T \rightarrow S$ of $R$ algebras such that $u v=1_{T}$; in particular $v$ is an injection. Clearly $v$ induces a bijection on the cotangent spaces, so $v$ is also a surjection (1.1). Hence $v$ is an isomorphism of $T=R\left[\left[X_{1}, \ldots, X_{n}\right]\right]$ with $S$.

Conversely, if $S$ is a power series ring over $R$, then it is obvious that $h_{S} \rightarrow h_{R}$ is smooth.

The proofs of (ii), (iii), (iv) are completely formal and are left to the reader.
nodes.statement_short: Lift $S\to T/(t^2+rT)$ step by step via smoothness to $u:S\to T$, build a section $v$, and use Lemma 1.1 to get $S\cong T$; (ii)-(iv) formal.

nodes.statement: (2.6) Notation. Let $k[\varepsilon]$, where $\varepsilon^{2}=0$, denote the ring of dual numbers over $k$.

nodes.name: tangent space of a functor
nodes.statement: For any functor $F$, the set $F(k[\varepsilon])$ is called the tangent space to $F$, and is denoted by $t_{F}$.

nodes.name: tangent space of h_R
nodes.statement:
It is easy to see that if $F=h_{R}$, then there is a canonical isomorphism $t_{F} \cong t_{R}$ :

$$
t_{R} \cong \operatorname{Hom}_{\Lambda}(R, k[\varepsilon]) .
$$
conclusions: there is a canonical isomorphism $t_{F} \cong t_{R}$

nodes.name: pro-representable hull
nodes.statement: Definition 2.7. A pro-couple $(R, \xi)$ for a functor $F$ is called a pro-representable hull of $F$, or just a hull of $F$, if the induced map $h_{R} \rightarrow F$ is smooth (2.2), and if in addition the induced map $t_{R} \rightarrow t_{F}$ of tangent spaces is a bijection.
differentia: the induced map $h_{R} \rightarrow F$ is smooth (2.2)
the induced map $t_{R} \rightarrow t_{F}$ of tangent spaces is a bijection
also_stated_at: If $R$ is chosen suitably "minimal" then $R$ is called a "hull" of $F ; R$ is then unique up to noncanonical isomorphism.
nodes.statement_short: A hull of $F$ is a pro-couple $(R,\xi)$ with $h_R\to F$ smooth and $t_R\to t_F$ bijective.

nodes.name: Remark 2.8 (pro-representing pairs are hulls)
nodes.statement: (2.8) Notice that if $(R, \xi)$ pro-represents $F$ then $(R, \xi)$ is a hull of $F$. In this case $(R, \xi)$ is unique up to canonical isomorphism.
conclusions: $(R, \xi)$ is a hull of $F$

nodes.statement:
Proof of 2.11. (1) Suppose $F$ satisfies conditions $\left(\mathrm{H}_{1}\right),\left(\mathrm{H}_{2}\right),\left(\mathrm{H}_{3}\right)$. Let $t_{1}, \ldots, t_{r}$ be a dual basis of $t_{F}$, put $S=\Lambda\left[\left[T_{1}, \ldots, T_{r}\right]\right]$, and let $\boldsymbol{n}$ be the maximal ideal of $S$. $R$ will be constructed as the projective limit of successive quotients of $S$. To begin, let $R_{2}=S /\left(n^{2}+\mu S\right) \cong k[\varepsilon] \times_{k} \cdots \times_{k} k[\varepsilon]$ ( $r$ times). By $\left(\mathrm{H}_{2}\right)$ there exists $\xi_{2} \in F\left(R_{2}\right)$ which induces a bijection between $t_{R_{2}}\left(\cong \operatorname{Hom}\left(R_{2}, k[\varepsilon]\right)\right)$ and $t_{F}$. Suppose we have found $\left(R_{q}, \xi_{q}\right)$, where $R_{q}=S / J_{q}$. We seek an ideal $J_{q+1}$ in $S$, minimal among those ideals $J$ in $S$ satisfying the conditions (a) $n J_{q} \subseteq J \subseteq J_{q}$, (b) $\xi_{q}$ lifts to $S / J$. Since the set $\mathscr{S}$ of such ideals corresponds to a certain collection of vector subspaces of $J_{q} /\left(n J_{q}\right)$, it suffices to show that $\mathscr{S}$ is stable under pairwise intersection. But if\\
$J$ and $K$ are in $\mathscr{S}$, we may enlarge $J$, say, so that $J+K=J_{q}$, without changing the intersection $J \cap K$. Then

$$
S / J \times_{S / J_{q}} S / K \cong S /(J \cap K)
$$

so that by $\left(\mathrm{H}_{1}\right)$ (see (2.14)) we may conclude that $J \cap K$ is in $\mathscr{S}$. Let $J_{q+1}$ be the intersection of the members of $\mathscr{S}$, put $R_{q+1}=S / J_{q+1}$, and pick any $\xi_{q+1} \in F\left(R_{q+1}\right)$ which projects onto $\xi_{q} \in F\left(R_{q}\right)$.

Now let $J$ be the intersection of all the $J_{q}$ 's $(q=2,3, \ldots)$ and let $R=S / J$. Since $n^{q} \subseteq J_{q}$, the $J_{q} / J$ form a base for the topology in $R$, so that $R=$ proj $\operatorname{Lim} S / J_{q}$, and it is legitimate to set $\xi=$ proj $\operatorname{Lim} \xi_{q} \in \hat{F}(R)$. Notice that $t_{F} \cong t_{R}$, by choice of $R_{2}$.

We claim now that $h_{R} \rightarrow F$ is smooth. Let $p:\left(A^{\prime}, \eta^{\prime}\right) \rightarrow(A, \eta)$ be a morphism of couples, where $p$ is a small extension, $A=A^{\prime} / I$, and let $u:(R, \xi) \rightarrow(A, \eta)$ be a given morphism. We have to lift $u$ to a morphism $(R, \xi) \rightarrow\left(A^{\prime}, \eta^{\prime}\right)$. For this it suffices to find a $u^{\prime}: R \rightarrow A^{\prime}$ such that $p u^{\prime}=u$. In fact, we have a transitive action of $t_{F} \otimes I$ on $F(p)^{-1}(\eta)$ (resp. $h_{R}(p)^{-1}(\eta)$ ) by (2.15); thus, given such a $u^{\prime}$, there exists $\sigma \in t_{F} \otimes I$ such that $\left[F\left(u^{\prime}\right)(\xi)\right]^{\sigma}=\eta^{\prime}$, so that $v^{\prime}=\left(u^{\prime}\right)^{\sigma}$ will satisfy $F\left(v^{\prime}\right)(\xi)=\eta^{\prime}$, $p v^{\prime}=u$.

Now $u$ factors as $(R, \xi) \rightarrow\left(R_{q}, \xi_{q}\right) \rightarrow(A, \eta)$ for some $q$. Thus it suffices to complete the diagram\\
\includegraphics[max width=\textwidth, alt={}, center]{133f4430-1007-4a22-9674-9093b9475bf3-07_216_313_1247_671}\\
or equivalently, the diagram\\
\includegraphics[max width=\textwidth, alt={}, center]{133f4430-1007-4a22-9674-9093b9475bf3-07_223_596_1595_519}\\
where $w$ has been chosen so as to make the square commute. If the small extension $p r_{1}$ has a section, then $v$ obviously exists. Otherwise, by 1.4 (ii), $p r_{1}$ is essential, so $w$ is a surjection. By $\left(\mathrm{H}_{1}\right)$, applied to the projections of $R_{q} \times_{A} A^{\prime}$ on its factors, $\xi_{q} \in F\left(R_{q}\right)$ lifts back to $R_{q} \times_{A} A^{\prime}$, so ker $w \supseteq J_{q+1}$, by choice of $J_{q+1}$. Thus $w$ factors through $S / J_{q+1}=R_{q+1}$, and $v$ exists. This completes the proof that $(R, \xi)$ is a hull of $F$.

Conversely, suppose that a pro-couple $(R, \xi)$ is a hull of $F$. To verify $\left(\mathrm{H}_{1}\right)$, let $p^{\prime}:\left(A^{\prime}, \eta^{\prime}\right) \rightarrow(A, \eta)$ and $p^{\prime \prime}:\left(A^{\prime \prime}, \eta^{\prime \prime}\right) \rightarrow(A, \eta)$ be morphisms of couples, where $p^{\prime \prime}$\\
is a surjection. Since $h_{R} \rightarrow F$ is surjective, there exists a $u^{\prime}:(R, \xi) \rightarrow\left(A^{\prime}, \eta^{\prime}\right)$, and hence by smoothness applied to $p^{\prime \prime}$, there exists $u^{\prime \prime}:(R, \xi) \rightarrow\left(A^{\prime \prime}, \eta^{\prime \prime}\right)$ rendering the following diagram commutative:\\
\includegraphics[max width=\textwidth, alt={}, center]{133f4430-1007-4a22-9674-9093b9475bf3-08_421_627_507_519}\\
Therefore $\zeta=F\left(u^{\prime} \times u^{\prime \prime}\right)(\xi)$ projects onto $\eta^{\prime}$ and $\eta^{\prime \prime}$, so that $\left(\mathrm{H}_{1}\right)$ is satisfied.\\
Now suppose $(A, \eta)=(k, e)$, and $A^{\prime \prime}=k[\varepsilon]$. If $\zeta_{1}$ and $\zeta_{2}$ in $F\left(A^{\prime} \times_{k} k[\varepsilon]\right)$ have the same projections $\eta^{\prime}$ and $\eta^{\prime \prime}$ on the factors, then choosing $u^{\prime}$ as above we get morphisms

$$

$$

by smoothness applied to the projection of $A^{\prime} \times_{k} k[\varepsilon]$ on $A^{\prime}$. Since $t_{F} \cong t_{R}$ we have $u_{1}=u_{2}$, so that $\zeta_{1}=\zeta_{2}$, which proves $\left(\mathrm{H}_{2}\right)$. The isomorphism $t_{R} \cong t_{F}$ also proves $\left(\mathrm{H}_{3}\right)$.\\
(2) Suppose now that $F$ satisfies conditions $\left(\mathrm{H}_{1}\right)$ through $\left(\mathrm{H}_{4}\right)$. By part (1) we know that $F$ has a hull $(R, \xi)$. We shall prove that $h_{R}(A) \xrightarrow{\sim} F(A)$ by induction on length $A$. Consider a small extension $p: A^{\prime} \rightarrow A=A^{\prime} \mid I$, and assume that $h_{R}(A) \xrightarrow{\sim} F(A)$. For each $\eta \in F(A), h_{R}(p)^{-1}(\eta)$ and $F(p)^{-1}(\eta)$ are both formally principal homogeneous spaces under $t_{F} \otimes I(2.15)$; since $h_{R}\left(A^{\prime}\right)$ maps onto $F\left(A^{\prime}\right)$, we have $h_{R}\left(A^{\prime}\right) \xrightarrow{\sim} F\left(A^{\prime}\right)$, which proves the induction step.

The necessity of the four conditions has already been noted.

nodes.statement_short: $R_2=S/(n^2+\mu S)$ and $\xi_2$ from (H2).

nodes.name: Inductive choice of J_{q+1}
nodes.statement: Suppose we have found $\left(R_{q}, \xi_{q}\right)$, where $R_{q}=S / J_{q}$. We seek an ideal $J_{q+1}$ in $S$, minimal among those ideals $J$ in $S$ satisfying the conditions (a) $n J_{q} \subseteq J \subseteq J_{q}$, (b) $\xi_{q}$ lifts to $S / J$.
nodes.statement_short: Seek $J_{q+1}$ minimal with $nJ_q\subseteq J\subseteq J_q$ and $\xi_q$ lifting.

nodes.name: Stability under intersection
nodes.statement:
Since the set $\mathscr{S}$ of such ideals corresponds to a certain collection of vector subspaces of $J_{q} /\left(n J_{q}\right)$, it suffices to show that $\mathscr{S}$ is stable under pairwise intersection. But if\\
$J$ and $K$ are in $\mathscr{S}$, we may enlarge $J$, say, so that $J+K=J_{q}$, without changing the intersection $J \cap K$. Then

$$
S / J \times_{S / J_{q}} S / K \cong S /(J \cap K)
$$

so that by $\left(\mathrm{H}_{1}\right)$ (see (2.14)) we may conclude that $J \cap K$ is in $\mathscr{S}$.
nodes.statement_short: Using (H1) via (2.14), the set of such ideals is closed under intersection.

nodes.name: Define R_{q+1} and pass to the limit
nodes.statement:
Let $J_{q+1}$ be the intersection of the members of $\mathscr{S}$, put $R_{q+1}=S / J_{q+1}$, and pick any $\xi_{q+1} \in F\left(R_{q+1}\right)$ which projects onto $\xi_{q} \in F\left(R_{q}\right)$.

Now let $J$ be the intersection of all the $J_{q}$ 's $(q=2,3, \ldots)$ and let $R=S / J$. Since $n^{q} \subseteq J_{q}$, the $J_{q} / J$ form a base for the topology in $R$, so that $R=$ proj $\operatorname{Lim} S / J_{q}$, and it is legitimate to set $\xi=$ proj $\operatorname{Lim} \xi_{q} \in \hat{F}(R)$. Notice that $t_{F} \cong t_{R}$, by choice of $R_{2}$.
nodes.statement_short: Take $J_{q+1}$ the intersection, lift $\xi_q$, and set $R=\varprojlim S/J_q$ with $t_F\cong t_R$.

nodes.name: Claim: h_R -> F smooth
nodes.statement: We claim now that $h_{R} \rightarrow F$ is smooth. Let $p:\left(A^{\prime}, \eta^{\prime}\right) \rightarrow(A, \eta)$ be a morphism of couples, where $p$ is a small extension, $A=A^{\prime} / I$, and let $u:(R, \xi) \rightarrow(A, \eta)$ be a given morphism. We have to lift $u$ to a morphism $(R, \xi) \rightarrow\left(A^{\prime}, \eta^{\prime}\right)$. For this it suffices to find a $u^{\prime}: R \rightarrow A^{\prime}$ such that $p u^{\prime}=u$. In fact, we have a transitive action of $t_{F} \otimes I$ on $F(p)^{-1}(\eta)$ (resp. $h_{R}(p)^{-1}(\eta)$ ) by (2.15); thus, given such a $u^{\prime}$, there exists $\sigma \in t_{F} \otimes I$ such that $\left[F\left(u^{\prime}\right)(\xi)\right]^{\sigma}=\eta^{\prime}$, so that $v^{\prime}=\left(u^{\prime}\right)^{\sigma}$ will satisfy $F\left(v^{\prime}\right)(\xi)=\eta^{\prime}$, $p v^{\prime}=u$.
nodes.statement_short: Reduce smoothness to lifting $u$ through small extensions.

nodes.name: Set up lifting problem
nodes.statement: Let $p:\left(A^{\prime}, \eta^{\prime}\right) \rightarrow(A, \eta)$ be a morphism of couples, where $p$ is a small extension, $A=A^{\prime} / I$, and let $u:(R, \xi) \rightarrow(A, \eta)$ be a given morphism. We have to lift $u$ to a morphism $(R, \xi) \rightarrow\left(A^{\prime}, \eta^{\prime}\right)$.
nodes.statement_short: Given a small extension of couples, lift $u$.

nodes.name: Reduce to a ring lift
nodes.statement: For this it suffices to find a $u^{\prime}: R \rightarrow A^{\prime}$ such that $p u^{\prime}=u$. In fact, we have a transitive action of $t_{F} \otimes I$ on $F(p)^{-1}(\eta)$ (resp. $h_{R}(p)^{-1}(\eta)$ ) by (2.15); thus, given such a $u^{\prime}$, there exists $\sigma \in t_{F} \otimes I$ such that $\left[F\left(u^{\prime}\right)(\xi)\right]^{\sigma}=\eta^{\prime}$, so that $v^{\prime}=\left(u^{\prime}\right)^{\sigma}$ will satisfy $F\left(v^{\prime}\right)(\xi)=\eta^{\prime}$, $p v^{\prime}=u$.
nodes.statement_short: Transitive action of $t_F\otimes I$ (2.15) lets any ring lift be corrected to a couple lift.

nodes.name: Factor through R_q
nodes.statement:
Now $u$ factors as $(R, \xi) \rightarrow\left(R_{q}, \xi_{q}\right) \rightarrow(A, \eta)$ for some $q$. Thus it suffices to complete the diagram\\
\includegraphics[max width=\textwidth, alt={}, center]{133f4430-1007-4a22-9674-9093b9475bf3-07_216_313_1247_671}\\
or equivalently, the diagram\\
\includegraphics[max width=\textwidth, alt={}, center]{133f4430-1007-4a22-9674-9093b9475bf3-07_223_596_1595_519}\\
where $w$ has been chosen so as to make the square commute.
nodes.statement_short: Reduce to completing a diagram through $R_q$.

nodes.name: Case: section exists
nodes.statement: If the small extension $p r_{1}$ has a section, then $v$ obviously exists.
nodes.statement_short: If $pr_1$ has a section, $v$ exists.

nodes.name: Case: essential
nodes.statement: Otherwise, by 1.4 (ii), $p r_{1}$ is essential, so $w$ is a surjection. By $\left(\mathrm{H}_{1}\right)$, applied to the projections of $R_{q} \times_{A} A^{\prime}$ on its factors, $\xi_{q} \in F\left(R_{q}\right)$ lifts back to $R_{q} \times_{A} A^{\prime}$, so ker $w \supseteq J_{q+1}$, by choice of $J_{q+1}$. Thus $w$ factors through $S / J_{q+1}=R_{q+1}$, and $v$ exists. This completes the proof that $(R, \xi)$ is a hull of $F$.
nodes.statement_short: Otherwise $pr_1$ is essential by Lemma 1.4(ii), and minimality of $J_{q+1}$ gives the factorisation.

nodes.name: Converse: (H1)
nodes.statement:
Conversely, suppose that a pro-couple $(R, \xi)$ is a hull of $F$. To verify $\left(\mathrm{H}_{1}\right)$, let $p^{\prime}:\left(A^{\prime}, \eta^{\prime}\right) \rightarrow(A, \eta)$ and $p^{\prime \prime}:\left(A^{\prime \prime}, \eta^{\prime \prime}\right) \rightarrow(A, \eta)$ be morphisms of couples, where $p^{\prime \prime}$\\
is a surjection. Since $h_{R} \rightarrow F$ is surjective, there exists a $u^{\prime}:(R, \xi) \rightarrow\left(A^{\prime}, \eta^{\prime}\right)$, and hence by smoothness applied to $p^{\prime \prime}$, there exists $u^{\prime \prime}:(R, \xi) \rightarrow\left(A^{\prime \prime}, \eta^{\prime \prime}\right)$ rendering the following diagram commutative:\\
\includegraphics[max width=\textwidth, alt={}, center]{133f4430-1007-4a22-9674-9093b9475bf3-08_421_627_507_519}\\
Therefore $\zeta=F\left(u^{\prime} \times u^{\prime \prime}\right)(\xi)$ projects onto $\eta^{\prime}$ and $\eta^{\prime \prime}$, so that $\left(\mathrm{H}_{1}\right)$ is satisfied.
nodes.statement_short: A hull gives (H1) by smoothness.

nodes.name: Converse: (H2)
nodes.statement:
Now suppose $(A, \eta)=(k, e)$, and $A^{\prime \prime}=k[\varepsilon]$. If $\zeta_{1}$ and $\zeta_{2}$ in $F\left(A^{\prime} \times_{k} k[\varepsilon]\right)$ have the same projections $\eta^{\prime}$ and $\eta^{\prime \prime}$ on the factors, then choosing $u^{\prime}$ as above we get morphisms

$$
u^{\prime} \times u_{i}:(R, \xi) \rightarrow\left(A^{\prime} \times_{k} k[\varepsilon], \zeta_{i}\right), \quad i=1,2,
$$

by smoothness applied to the projection of $A^{\prime} \times_{k} k[\varepsilon]$ on $A^{\prime}$. Since $t_{F} \cong t_{R}$ we have $u_{1}=u_{2}$, so that $\zeta_{1}=\zeta_{2}$, which proves $\left(\mathrm{H}_{2}\right)$.
nodes.statement_short: Tangent bijection forces uniqueness, giving (H2).

nodes.name: Converse: (H3)
nodes.statement: The isomorphism $t_{R} \cong t_{F}$ also proves $\left(\mathrm{H}_{3}\right)$.
nodes.statement_short: $t_R\cong t_F$ gives finiteness (H3).

nodes.name: Part (2): pro-representability
nodes.statement: (2) Suppose now that $F$ satisfies conditions $\left(\mathrm{H}_{1}\right)$ through $\left(\mathrm{H}_{4}\right)$. By part (1) we know that $F$ has a hull $(R, \xi)$. We shall prove that $h_{R}(A) \xrightarrow{\sim} F(A)$ by induction on length $A$. Consider a small extension $p: A^{\prime} \rightarrow A=A^{\prime} \mid I$, and assume that $h_{R}(A) \xrightarrow{\sim} F(A)$. For each $\eta \in F(A), h_{R}(p)^{-1}(\eta)$ and $F(p)^{-1}(\eta)$ are both formally principal homogeneous spaces under $t_{F} \otimes I(2.15)$; since $h_{R}\left(A^{\prime}\right)$ maps onto $F\left(A^{\prime}\right)$, we have $h_{R}\left(A^{\prime}\right) \xrightarrow{\sim} F\left(A^{\prime}\right)$, which proves the induction step.
nodes.statement_short: Under (H4), induct on length to show $h_R\cong F$.

nodes.name: Hull from part (1)
nodes.statement: Suppose now that $F$ satisfies conditions $\left(\mathrm{H}_{1}\right)$ through $\left(\mathrm{H}_{4}\right)$. By part (1) we know that $F$ has a hull $(R, \xi)$.
nodes.statement_short: Part (1) gives a hull.

nodes.name: Plan induction
nodes.statement: We shall prove that $h_{R}(A) \xrightarrow{\sim} F(A)$ by induction on length $A$.
nodes.statement_short: Induct on length of $A$.

nodes.name: Inductive step
nodes.statement: Consider a small extension $p: A^{\prime} \rightarrow A=A^{\prime} \mid I$, and assume that $h_{R}(A) \xrightarrow{\sim} F(A)$. For each $\eta \in F(A), h_{R}(p)^{-1}(\eta)$ and $F(p)^{-1}(\eta)$ are both formally principal homogeneous spaces under $t_{F} \otimes I(2.15)$; since $h_{R}\left(A^{\prime}\right)$ maps onto $F\left(A^{\prime}\right)$, we have $h_{R}\left(A^{\prime}\right) \xrightarrow{\sim} F\left(A^{\prime}\right)$, which proves the induction step.
nodes.statement_short: Both fibres are principal homogeneous under $t_F\otimes I$ (2.15), so surjection is bijection.

nodes.name: Necessity
nodes.statement: The necessity of the four conditions has already been noted.
nodes.statement_short: Necessity was noted after the statement.

nodes.name: Picard group
nodes.statement: If $X$ is a prescheme, we define $\operatorname{Pic}(X)=H^{1}\left(X, \mathfrak{D}_{X}^{*}\right)$, the group of isomorphism classes of invertible (i.e., locally free of rank one) sheaves on $X$.

nodes.name: automorphisms of an invertible sheaf
nodes.statement: Recall that the group of automorphisms of an invertible sheaf is canonically isomorphic to $H^{0}\left(X, \mathfrak{O}_{X}^{*}\right)$.
conclusions: the group of automorphisms of an invertible sheaf is canonically isomorphic to $H^{0}\left(X, \mathfrak{O}_{X}^{*}\right)$

nodes.name: base change X_A and closed fibre X_0
nodes.statement: Now suppose $X$ is a prescheme over Spec $\Lambda$. We let $X_{A}$ abbreviate $X \times_{\operatorname{Spec} \Lambda} \operatorname{Spec} A$ for $A$ in $C$, and set $X_{0}=X_{k}$.

nodes.name: induced element eta tensor B
nodes.statement: If $\eta$ (resp. $L$ ) is an element of $\operatorname{Pic}\left(X_{A}\right)$ (resp. an invertible sheaf on $X_{A}$ ) and $A \rightarrow B$ is a morphism in $C$, let $\eta \otimes_{A} B$ (resp. $L \otimes_{A} B$ ) denote the induced element of $\operatorname{Pic}\left(X_{B}\right)$ (resp. induced invertible sheaf on $X_{B}$ ).

nodes.name: Picard functor P
nodes.statement:
Let $\xi_{0}$ be an element of $\operatorname{Pic}\left(X_{0}\right)$ fixed once and for all in this discussion, and let\\
$\boldsymbol{P}(A)$ be the subset of $\operatorname{Pic}\left(X_{A}\right)$ consisting of those $\eta$ such that $\eta \otimes_{A} k=\xi_{0}$.
nodes.statement_short: $P(A)$: elements of $\operatorname{Pic}(X_A)$ restricting to a fixed $\xi_0$ on $X_0$.

nodes.name: Proposition 3.2 (pro-representability of the Picard functor)
nodes.statement:
Proposition 3.2. Assume

\begin{itemize}
  \item[(i)] $X$ is flat over $\Lambda$,
  \item[(ii)] $A \xrightarrow{\sim} H^{\circ}\left(X_{A}, \mathfrak{O}_{X_{A}}\right)$ for each $A \in C$,
  \item[(iii)] $\operatorname{dim}_{k} H^{1}\left(X_{0}, \mathfrak{O}_{X_{0}}\right)<\infty$.
\end{itemize}

Then $\boldsymbol{P}$ is pro-representable by a pro-couple $(R, \xi)$; furthermore $t_{R} \cong H^{1}\left(X_{0}, \mathfrak{O}_{X_{0}}\right)$.
conclusions: $\boldsymbol{P}$ is pro-representable by a pro-couple $(R, \xi)$
$t_{R} \cong H^{1}\left(X_{0}, \mathfrak{O}_{X_{0}}\right)$
nodes.statement_short: Under flatness, $H^0$ and finiteness conditions, the Picard functor is pro-representable with tangent space $H^1(X_0,\mathcal O)$.

nodes.name: equivalent form of condition (ii) of Proposition 3.2
nodes.statement: Notice that condition (ii) is equivalent to the condition $k \longrightarrow H^{0}\left(X_{0}, \mathfrak{D}_{X_{0}}\right)$, in view of (i).
conclusions: condition (ii) is equivalent to the condition $k \longrightarrow H^{0}\left(X_{0}, \mathfrak{D}_{X_{0}}\right)$

nodes.name: Proof of the equivalent form of condition (ii)
nodes.statement: In fact, by flatness, the functor $M \mapsto T(M)=H^{0}\left(X, \mathfrak{O}_{X} \otimes M\right)$ of $\Lambda$ modules is left exact. A standard five lemma type of argument then shows that the natural map $M \rightarrow T(M)$ is an isomorphism for all $M$ of finite length.
nodes.statement_short: Flatness makes $M\mapsto H^0(X,\mathcal O_X\otimes M)$ left exact; five-lemma argument on finite length modules.

nodes.name: Lemma 3.3 (nilpotent Nakayama for flat modules)
nodes.statement: Lemma 3.3. Let $A$ be a ring, $J$ a nilpotent ideal in $A$, and $u: M \rightarrow N$ a homomorphism of $A$ modules, with $N$ flat over $A$. If $\bar{u}: M / J M \rightarrow N / J N$ is an isomorphism, then $u$ is an isomorphism.
assumptions: $u: M \rightarrow N$ a homomorphism of $A$ modules, with $N$ flat over $A$
$\bar{u}: M / J M \rightarrow N / J N$ is an isomorphism
conclusions: $u$ is an isomorphism

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 3.3
nodes.statement:
Proof. Let $K=$ coker $u$ and tensor the exact sequence «

$$
M \rightarrow N \rightarrow K \rightarrow 0
$$

with $A / J$. Then we find $K / J K=0$, which implies $K=0$, since $J$ is nilpotent. Thus, if $K^{\prime}=$ ker $u$, we get an exact sequence

$$
0 \rightarrow K^{\prime} / J K^{\prime} \rightarrow M / J M \rightarrow N / J N \rightarrow 0
$$

by the flatness of $N$. Hence $K^{\prime}=0$, so that $u$ is an isomorphism.
nodes.statement_short: Nakayama for nilpotent $J$ kills the cokernel; flatness of $N$ then kills the kernel.

nodes.name: Tensor cokernel sequence
nodes.statement:
Let $K=$ coker $u$ and tensor the exact sequence «

$$
M \rightarrow N \rightarrow K \rightarrow 0
$$

with $A / J$.
nodes.statement_short: Tensor $M\to N\to K\to0$ with $A/J$.

nodes.name: Cokernel vanishes
nodes.statement: Then we find $K / J K=0$, which implies $K=0$, since $J$ is nilpotent.
nodes.statement_short: $K/JK=0$ and nilpotence give $K=0$.

nodes.name: Kernel sequence by flatness
nodes.statement:
Thus, if $K^{\prime}=$ ker $u$, we get an exact sequence

$$
0 \rightarrow K^{\prime} / J K^{\prime} \rightarrow M / J M \rightarrow N / J N \rightarrow 0
$$

by the flatness of $N$.
nodes.statement_short: Flatness gives exactness with the kernel.

nodes.name: Conclude
nodes.statement: Hence $K^{\prime}=0$, so that $u$ is an isomorphism.
nodes.statement_short: Kernel vanishes, so $u$ is an isomorphism.

nodes.name: Lemma 3.4 (flatness over fibre products)
nodes.statement:
Lemma 3.4. Consider a commutative diagram\\
\includegraphics[max width=\textwidth, alt={}, center]{133f4430-1007-4a22-9674-9093b9475bf3-09_419_389_1601_651}\\
of compatible ring and module homomorphisms, where $B=A^{\prime} \times_{A} A^{\prime \prime}, N=M^{\prime} \times_{M} M^{\prime \prime}$ and $M^{\prime}$ (resp. $M^{\prime \prime}$ ) is a flat $A^{\prime}$ (resp. $A^{\prime \prime}$ ) module. Suppose

\begin{itemize}
  \item[(i)] $A^{\prime \prime} / J \xrightarrow{\sim} A$, where $J$ is a nilpotent ideal in $A^{\prime \prime}$,
  \item[(ii)] $u^{\prime}$ (resp. $u^{\prime \prime}$ ) induces $M^{\prime} \otimes_{A^{\prime}} A \xrightarrow{\sim} M\left(\right.$ resp. $\left.M^{\prime \prime} \otimes_{A^{\prime \prime}} A \xrightarrow{\sim} M\right)$.
\end{itemize}

Then $N$ is flat over $B$ and $p^{\prime}$ (resp. $p^{\prime \prime}$ ) induces $N \otimes_{B} A^{\prime} \xrightarrow{\sim} M^{\prime} \quad$ (resp. $\left.N \otimes_{B} A^{\prime \prime} \xrightarrow{\sim} M^{\prime \prime}\right)$.
assumptions: $B=A^{\prime} \times_{A} A^{\prime \prime}, N=M^{\prime} \times_{M} M^{\prime \prime}$ and $M^{\prime}$ (resp. $M^{\prime \prime}$ ) is a flat $A^{\prime}$ (resp. $A^{\prime \prime}$ ) module
$A^{\prime \prime} / J \xrightarrow{\sim} A$, where $J$ is a nilpotent ideal in $A^{\prime \prime}$
conclusions: $N$ is flat over $B$
nodes.statement_short: A fibre product of compatible flat modules over $A'\times_A A''$ (with $A''\to A$ a nilpotent thickening) is flat and restricts correctly.

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 3.4
nodes.statement:
Proof. We shall consider only the case where $M^{\prime}$ is actually a free $A^{\prime}$ module. (This case actually suffices for our purposes, since a simple application of Lemma 3.3 shows that a flat module over an Artin local ring is free.) Choose a basis $\left(x_{i}^{\prime}\right)_{i \in I}$ for $M^{\prime}$. Then by (ii) we find that $M$ is the free module on generators $u^{\prime}\left(x_{i}^{\prime}\right)$. Choosing $x_{i}^{\prime \prime} \in M^{\prime \prime}$ such that $u^{\prime \prime}\left(x_{i}^{\prime \prime}\right)=u^{\prime}\left(x_{i}^{\prime}\right)$, we get a map $\sum A^{\prime \prime} x_{i}^{\prime \prime} \rightarrow M^{\prime \prime}$ of $A^{\prime \prime}$ modules, whose reduction modulo the ideal $J$ is an isomorphism. Therefore $M^{\prime \prime}$ is free on generators $x_{i}^{\prime \prime}$ (Lemma 3.3) and it follows easily that $N=M^{\prime} \times_{M} M^{\prime \prime}$ is free on generators $x_{i}^{\prime} \times x_{i}^{\prime \prime}$, and that the projections on the factors induce isomorphisms

$$
N \otimes_{B} A^{\prime} \xrightarrow{\sim} M^{\prime}, \quad N \otimes_{B} A^{\prime \prime} \xrightarrow{\sim} M^{\prime \prime}
$$

as desired. (A similar argument for the case of general $M^{\prime}$ is given in [4, §1, Proposition 2].)
nodes.statement_short: Reduce to free $M'$; lift a basis to $M''$, freeness by Lemma 3.3, so $N$ is free on paired generators.

nodes.name: Reduce to free case
nodes.statement: We shall consider only the case where $M^{\prime}$ is actually a free $A^{\prime}$ module. (This case actually suffices for our purposes, since a simple application of Lemma 3.3 shows that a flat module over an Artin local ring is free.)
nodes.statement_short: Reduce to $M'$ free using Lemma 3.3.

nodes.name: Choose basis
nodes.statement: Choose a basis $\left(x_{i}^{\prime}\right)_{i \in I}$ for $M^{\prime}$. Then by (ii) we find that $M$ is the free module on generators $u^{\prime}\left(x_{i}^{\prime}\right)$.
nodes.statement_short: Basis of $M'$ gives basis of $M$.

nodes.name: Lift generators to M''
nodes.statement: Choosing $x_{i}^{\prime \prime} \in M^{\prime \prime}$ such that $u^{\prime \prime}\left(x_{i}^{\prime \prime}\right)=u^{\prime}\left(x_{i}^{\prime}\right)$, we get a map $\sum A^{\prime \prime} x_{i}^{\prime \prime} \rightarrow M^{\prime \prime}$ of $A^{\prime \prime}$ modules, whose reduction modulo the ideal $J$ is an isomorphism.
nodes.statement_short: Lift generators to $M''$; map is iso mod $J$.

nodes.name: Conclude freeness
nodes.statement:
Therefore $M^{\prime \prime}$ is free on generators $x_{i}^{\prime \prime}$ (Lemma 3.3) and it follows easily that $N=M^{\prime} \times_{M} M^{\prime \prime}$ is free on generators $x_{i}^{\prime} \times x_{i}^{\prime \prime}$, and that the projections on the factors induce isomorphisms

$$
N \otimes_{B} A^{\prime} \xrightarrow{\sim} M^{\prime}, \quad N \otimes_{B} A^{\prime \prime} \xrightarrow{\sim} M^{\prime \prime}
$$

as desired. (A similar argument for the case of general $M^{\prime}$ is given in [4, §1, Proposition 2].)
nodes.statement_short: By Lemma 3.3 $M''$ is free, so $N$ is free with the right reductions.

nodes.name: Corollary 3.6 (uniqueness of the glued module)
nodes.statement:
Corollary 3.6. With the notations as above, let $L$ be a $B$ module which may be inserted in a commutative diagram\\
\includegraphics[max width=\textwidth, alt={}, center]{133f4430-1007-4a22-9674-9093b9475bf3-10_401_424_1149_622}\\
where $q^{\prime}$ induces $L \otimes_{B} A^{\prime} \xrightarrow{\sim} M^{\prime}$. Then the canonical morphism $q^{\prime} \times q^{\prime \prime}: L \rightarrow N$ $=M^{\prime} \times_{M} M^{\prime \prime}$ is an isomorphism.
assumptions: $L$ be a $B$ module which may be inserted in a commutative diagram
conclusions: the canonical morphism $q^{\prime} \times q^{\prime \prime}: L \rightarrow N$ $=M^{\prime} \times_{M} M^{\prime \prime}$ is an isomorphism

nodes.name: Proof of Corollary 3.6
nodes.statement: Proof. Apply Lemma 3.3 to the morphism $u=q^{\prime} \times q^{\prime \prime}$.
nodes.statement_short: Apply Lemma 3.3 to $q'\times q''$.

nodes.name: counterexample to Lemma 3.4 without surjectivity
nodes.statement: Remark. Lemma 3.4 is false, in general, if neither $A^{\prime \prime} \rightarrow A$ nor $A^{\prime} \rightarrow A$ is assumed surjective. For example, let $A^{\prime}$ be a sublocal ring of the local ring $A$, and map $A_{1}=A^{\prime \prime}$ into $A$ by inclusion. Let $a$ be a unit of $A$ such that the ideal $\left(a A^{\prime}\right) \cap A^{\prime}$ of $A^{\prime}$ is not flat ( = free) over $A^{\prime}$. (In $C_{\Lambda}$ one could take $A=k[t] /\left(t^{3}\right), A^{\prime}=k\left[t^{2}\right]$, $a=1+t$.) Let $M^{\prime}=M^{\prime \prime}=A^{\prime}, \quad M=A, \quad u^{\prime}=$ inclusion, $u^{\prime \prime}=$ multiplication by $a^{-1}$. Then $B \cong A^{\prime}$, while $N \cong\left(a A^{\prime}\right) \cap A^{\prime}$ is not flat over $B$.
nodes.statement_short: Without surjectivity of $A''\to A$ or $A'\to A$, Lemma 3.4 fails, e.g. $A=k[t]/(t^3)$, $A'=k[t^2]$, $a=1+t$.

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition 3.2
nodes.statement:
Proof of Proposition 3.2. Let $u^{\prime}:\left(A^{\prime}, \eta^{\prime}\right) \rightarrow(A, \eta), u^{\prime \prime}:\left(A^{\prime \prime}, \eta^{\prime \prime}\right) \rightarrow(A, \eta)$ be morphisms of couples, where $u^{\prime \prime}$ is a surjection. Let $L^{\prime}, L, L^{\prime \prime}$ be corresponding invertible sheaves on $X^{\prime}=X_{A^{\prime}}, Y=X_{A}$, and $X^{\prime \prime}=X_{A^{\prime \prime}}$. Then we have morphisms $p^{\prime}: L^{\prime} \rightarrow L$, $p^{\prime \prime}: L^{\prime \prime} \rightarrow L$ (of sheaves on the topological space $\left|X_{0}\right|$, compatible with $\mathfrak{O}_{X^{\prime}} \rightarrow \mathfrak{D}_{Y}$, $\mathfrak{O}_{X^{\prime \prime}} \rightarrow \mathfrak{D}_{Y}$ ) which induce isomorphisms $L^{\prime} \otimes_{A^{\prime}} A \xrightarrow{\sim} L, L^{\prime \prime} \otimes_{A^{\prime \prime}} A \xrightarrow{\sim} L$.

Let $B=A^{\prime} \times{ }_{A} A^{\prime \prime}$, and let $Z=X_{B}$. Then we have a commutative diagram\\
\includegraphics[max width=\textwidth, alt={}, center]{133f4430-1007-4a22-9674-9093b9475bf3-11_429_439_401_624}\\
of sheaves on $\left|X_{0}\right|$; thus by Corollary 3.6 there is a canonical isomorphism $\mathfrak{O}_{Z} \xrightarrow{\sim} \mathfrak{D}_{X^{\prime}} \times_{\mathfrak{O}_{Y}} \mathfrak{O}_{X^{\prime \prime}}$, where $\mathfrak{O}_{X^{\prime}} \times_{\mathfrak{O}_{Y}} \mathfrak{O}_{X^{\prime \prime}}$ is the sheaf of $B$-algebras whose sections over an open $U$ in $\left|X_{0}\right|$ are given by

$$
\mathfrak{O}_{X^{\prime}} \times \mathfrak{D}_{Y} \mathfrak{O}_{X^{\prime \prime}}(U)=\mathfrak{O}_{X^{\prime}}(U) \times_{\mathfrak{D}_{Y}(U)} \mathfrak{O}_{X^{\prime \prime}}(U) .
$$

Hence $N=L^{\prime} \times_{L} L^{\prime \prime}$ is a sheaf on $Z$, obviously invertible, and the projections of $N$ on $L^{\prime}$ and $L^{\prime \prime}$ induce isomorphisms $N \otimes_{B} A^{\prime} \xrightarrow{\sim} L^{\prime}, N \otimes_{B} A^{\prime \prime} \xrightarrow{\sim} L^{\prime \prime}$ by Lemma 3.4.\\
If $M$ is another invertible sheaf on $Z$ for which there exist isomorphisms

$$
M \otimes A^{\prime} \xrightarrow{\sim} L^{\prime}, \quad M \otimes A^{\prime \prime} \xrightarrow{\sim} L^{\prime \prime},
$$

we have morphisms $q^{\prime}: M \rightarrow L^{\prime}, q^{\prime \prime}: M \rightarrow L^{\prime \prime}$ which induce these isomorphisms, and thus a commutative diagram\\
\includegraphics[max width=\textwidth, alt={}, center]{133f4430-1007-4a22-9674-9093b9475bf3-11_248_436_1525_631}\\
Here $\theta$ is the automorphism of $L$ given by the composition

$$

Finally, letting $Y=X_{k[\varepsilon]}$, we have $\mathfrak{O}_{Y}=\mathfrak{D}_{X_{0}} \oplus \varepsilon \mathfrak{D}_{X_{0}}$, so there is a split exact sequence

nodes.statement:

of sheaves on $\left|X_{0}\right|$; thus by Corollary 3.6 there is a canonical isomorphism $\mathfrak{O}_{Z} \xrightarrow{\sim} \mathfrak{D}_{X^{\prime}} \times_{\mathfrak{O}_{Y}} \mathfrak{O}_{X^{\prime \prime}}$, where $\mathfrak{O}_{X^{\prime}} \times_{\mathfrak{O}_{Y}} \mathfrak{O}_{X^{\prime \prime}}$ is the sheaf of $B$-algebras whose sections over an open $U$ in $\left|X_{0}\right|$ are given by

nodes.statement:

nodes.name: Fix automorphism by hypothesis (ii)

nodes.name: infinitesimal deformation

To consider the condition $\left(\mathrm{H}_{4}\right)$, let $p:\left(A^{\prime}, \eta^{\prime}\right) \rightarrow(A, \eta)$ be a morphism of couples, where $p$ is a small extension. Lemma 3.8. The following are equivalent\\

\begin{equation*}

\end{equation*}


where $T^{0}$ is the sheaf of derivations of $\mathfrak{O}_{X}$, and $T^{1}$ is a (coherent) sheaf isomorphic to the sheaf of germs of deformations of $X / k$ to $k[\varepsilon]$. If $X$ is smooth over $k$, then $T^{0}=\Theta, T^{1}=0$. Thus, in summary
